case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlowe City Hotels (MBH) is a public limited company in the boutique hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 160 across six city-centre properties. Founded in 2008 by Daniel Okafor, it has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership and sells 24,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied apartment-night at an average selling price of $170. MBH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing and rebranding its properties, financed by a $500,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year and a variable cost of $70 a unit. MBH's guest satisfaction score has fallen to 3.9 out of 5 and absence among reception staff has reached 7%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Guest Report, Q4 2025: MBH logged 6,000 apartment-nights last quarter with 47 service complaints, up from 29 in the same quarter last year. The guest satisfaction score slipped to 3.9 out of 5 from 4.4, and 7% of reception shifts were uncovered through absence. Check-in averaged 6.8 minutes against a 4-minute promise. A survey of 820 past guests found 61% would pay $15 more for a refurbished suite and 54% book boutique hotels through review sites. Of 160 staff, 38 have not completed on-the-job refresher training; off-the-job customer-care courses at the city college cost $540 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and City Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising the cost of MBH's variable-rate $700,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% from $14.50 to $15.20 an hour from April 2026, increasing reception and housekeeping wage costs. (3) City business rates have risen 7.2%, while city visitor spending grew 4.1% and hotel energy costs rose 11.3% year-on-year.

questions.question_text: MBH plans to fund part of its refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MBH of using the $500,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, so MBH can commit the $500,000 to refurbishing six city-centre properties without adding to the interest burden on its $700,000 bank loan, especially as the base rate has risen to 4.75%. With fixed costs already at $600,000 a year and energy costs up 11.3%, avoiding debt service protects the $100 contribution earned on each of the 24,000 apartment-nights and leaves more cash to reverse the falling 3.9 guest satisfaction score.

Point 2: Share capital does not require collateral, so the properties themselves are not put at risk if the rebrand fails to attract bookings — a real concern while 7% of reception shifts are uncovered. As a public limited company, MBH can access equity investors more easily than a smaller firm, and the extra capital strengthens the balance sheet before the $1,200,000 programme. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders including founder Daniel Okafor, but the avoided interest and repayment obligations make the share issue attractive for a long-life refurbishment that will earn returns over many years.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MBH's funding and refurbishment.

questions.question_text: MBH is relaunching its boutique brand after refurbishment. Consider print press advertising, sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms, and social media travel influencers. Which should MBH choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print press advertising: Newspaper and magazine features can build credibility for a relaunched boutique brand and reach older, higher-spending city visitors. However, print has no direct booking link, its reach is hard to measure, and the cost of full-page colour adverts in national titles would be high for a business already funding a $1,200,000 refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Much of the readership will not be in MBH's six cities, so wastage is significant.

Sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms: Paid placement on the sites where 54% of surveyed guests say they book boutique hotels would intercept customers at the moment of decision and drive measurable bookings for the refurbished suites. The downside is cost per click on competitive city keywords and dependence on a third-party platform that also lists rivals; MBH would be renting visibility rather than owning a direct relationship with guests, which weakens the brand it is trying to rebuild.

Social media travel influencers: Design, food and city-break influencers can showcase the refurbished suites visually to the 54% who book via review sites and the 61% who would pay $15 more for a refurbished suite. Content is shareable, targeting is precise and cost per engagement is lower than print, though results take time to build and depend on credible, well-matched influencers.

Recommendation: MBH should choose sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms as the primary channel, reinforced by a smaller influencer campaign. Platform sponsorship converts the 54% who already book through review sites at the decision point, which is what the $1,200,000 refurbishment needs to fill 24,000 apartment-nights. Print is rejected as unmeasurable and costly while MBH services a $700,000 loan and $600,000 fixed costs; influencers alone are rejected because they build awareness more slowly than booking-platform placement. The $500,000 share issue can fund the launch without more debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to MBH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MBH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MBH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: MBH's guest satisfaction score has fallen and reception absence is high. Explain two benefits for MBH of its laissez-faire leadership style in improving this situation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives MBH's experienced reception teams freedom to solve guest problems immediately, which is valuable when satisfaction has slipped to 3.9 out of 5 and 47 service complaints were logged. Staff closest to the guest can offer an on-the-spot remedy rather than waiting for a manager, speeding up a response to the 6.8-minute check-in and helping lift the score back towards 4.4. Faster decisions improve the guest experience without adding management layers to a flat structure of 160 employees.

Point 2: Delegating decisions can raise motivation and reduce the 7% reception absence, because trusted employees feel ownership of their work rather than being closely supervised. Higher autonomy often improves job satisfaction, encouraging staff to protect their shifts and lowering the disruption caused by uncovered desks. That continuity supports the $1,200,000 rebrand, since consistent service is needed to justify the $15 premium that 61% of surveyed guests say they would pay. Laissez-faire leadership therefore attacks both the satisfaction decline and the absence problem through faster local decisions and greater staff commitment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MBH's satisfaction score, absence and premium pricing.

questions.question_text: MBH needs to train 38 staff in customer care after the refurbishment. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job training at the city college. Which should MBH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the reception desk uses MBH's own systems and real guest interactions, so the 38 staff learn exactly the behaviours needed to lift the 3.9 satisfaction score and shorten the 6.8-minute check-in. Training while working avoids course fees and keeps all six properties staffed, important while 7% of reception shifts are already uncovered and the company services a $700,000 loan. Its weakness is that trainers are working colleagues whose own duties suffer, and inconsistent coaching could leave the 47 complaints unresolved.

Off-the-job training: The city college customer-care course at $540 per employee gives structured, up-to-date service skills and a recognised certificate for all 38 staff, costing 38 × $540 = $20,520 in total — affordable within the $500,000 share issue and small beside the $1,200,000 refurbishment. It removes employees from the desks for several days, which may worsen uncovered shifts, and generic content may not reflect MBH's boutique brand standards, so some on-site reinforcement would still be needed.

Decision: MBH should choose off-the-job training for the 38 staff, followed by short on-the-job coaching once they return. The formal course gives the consistent service standard needed to justify the $15 premium and repair the 3.9 satisfaction score, and $20,520 is modest against the investment. On-the-job training alone is rejected because the same 7% absence problem would leave trainers overstretched and spread uneven practice across six sites; the shortfall of cover can be managed with temporary rotas while staff attend college. MBH should then compare complaint numbers and the satisfaction score before and after training to confirm that the $20,520 delivers a measurable improvement in service.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MBH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of MBH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, cover and brand standards.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MBH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($170 − $70) = $600,000 ÷ $100 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 apartment-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $170 − $70 = $100. Answer: contribution per unit is $100.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MBH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 24,000 apartment-nights: MBH has a margin of safety of 24,000 − 6,000 = 18,000 units, so it can lose a large share of bookings during refurbishment disruption before covering its $600,000 fixed costs.
2. Use contribution per unit of $100 to test pricing: the $15 premium for a refurbished suite would raise contribution to $115, showing the revenue needed to repay the $700,000 bank loan and justify the $1,200,000 programme.
3. Set sales targets for the rebrand: 7,000 extra apartment-nights at $100 contribution generate $700,000, enough to cover the loan principal, so managers can track progress by property.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $600,000 ÷ 24,000 + $70 = $95.00 an apartment-night and labour productivity of 24,000 ÷ 160 = 150 apartment-nights per employee, giving a baseline to measure the effect of the 11.3% energy cost rise and the 4.8% wage increase.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 18,000 apartment-nights; $15 premium and pricing analysis; loan-repayment volume targets for the $700,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $95.00 with labour productivity of 150 apartment-nights per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MBH's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MBH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.23 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $95,000 cash = $225,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $130,000 + $60,000 = $245,000. Coverage of short-term obligations 2024 = $225,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $245,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.29. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($225,000 − $40,000) ÷ $150,000 = $185,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.23; 2025 = ($245,000 − $55,000) ÷ $190,000 = $190,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Coverage of short-term obligations fell from 1.50 to 1.29 because current liabilities rose by $40,000 to $190,000 while current assets grew only $20,000. The stock-excluding measure fell more sharply, from 1.23 to 1.00, meaning MBH now has exactly enough liquid assets to cover its short-term debts with no cushion — risky while it services a $700,000 loan and plans a $1,200,000 refurbishment. Two movements explain this: cash fell from $95,000 to $60,000, and trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $130,000, tying up funds that could have paid suppliers. The small rise in inventories to $55,000 offers little protection because stock is the least liquid current asset.

Conclusion: MBH's financial position has not improved. Both measures are lower in 2025 and the fall in the stock-excluding measure to 1.00 is the stronger evidence of weaker underlying liquidity. MBH should chase outstanding receivables and slow the refurbishment drawdown until the cash balance is rebuilt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion that liquidity has not improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MBH of targeting the 54% of guests who book boutique hotels through review sites.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Focusing on the 54% of 820 surveyed guests who book boutique hotels through review sites lets MBH direct its relaunch spend at customers already in buying mode, supporting the $15 premium that 61% would pay for a refurbished suite. Strong reviews of the improved 3.9 satisfaction score can lift bookings towards the 24,000 apartment-nights needed to cover $600,000 fixed costs and service the $700,000 loan, while the reassurance of independently verified ratings helps justify the $1,200,000 refurbishment.

Disadvantage: Review sites charge commissions and give prominent placement to competing hotels, so MBH could see its $100 contribution per apartment-night reduced by platform fees and price comparison. A single run of poor reviews while refurbishment disruption continues could damage the brand before the score recovers from 3.9, and the platform controls the ranking, making MBH dependent on a channel it does not own. With energy costs up 11.3%, paying both commission and the 4.8% wage rise could squeeze margins; MBH should use review sites but also build direct bookings.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MBH's survey, satisfaction score and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in hotel energy costs will affect MBH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If MBH's $700,000 bank loan follows the base rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). This is a small fraction of the $600,000 fixed costs and can be substantially avoided by fixing the rate, although a higher base rate would make future finance for the $1,200,000 refurbishment more expensive. The direct annual impact is therefore limited.

Minimum wage increase (4.8%, to $15.20 an hour): Reception and housekeeping at MBH are hourly paid, so the rise feeds directly into wage costs and cannot be avoided. The insert provides no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the correct approach is qualitative, judged against the given 150 apartment-nights per employee and $100 contribution per unit. With satisfaction at 3.9 and 7% absence, MBH needs productivity to hold if the higher wage is to be absorbed without raising the $170 price.

Hotel energy costs (11.3%): These apply across all six properties and every one of the 24,000 apartment-nights. The insert does not break down the $70 variable cost, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% × $70 = $7.91 a unit, or about $189,840 a year (24,000 × $7.91). Even a smaller increase materially reduces the $100 contribution needed to repay the loan and fund the rebrand. The $15 premium for refurbished suites offers only partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in hotel energy costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 24,000 apartment-nights and directly threatens the $100 contribution that underpins the $1,200,000 refurbishment, whereas the interest rise is modest and can be hedged by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be absorbed through productivity and the $15 premium. Energy inflation therefore requires the most urgent action, such as efficiency investment and supplier renegotiation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MBH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MBH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of MBH with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
